title: Windows Management Instrumentation
summary: Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) is the management data and operations layer built into Windows, exposing a uniform interface that administrators and software can use to query system state and invoke methods. Adversaries abuse it as an execution channel: the WMI service accepts local and remote requests, and remote access is carried by transports such as Distributed Component Object Model (DCOM) over port 135 or Windows Remote Management (WinRM) over ports 5985 and 5986, so a request can start a process on another host using credentials already held. Executed payloads frequently appear as children of the WMI provider host rather than of an interactive shell, which hides them from users and from monitoring that only watches command prompts. The same interface supports discovery queries, service and scheduled task creation, and destructive actions such as deleting volume shadow copies to block recovery. Detection combines process creation telemetry, including Windows Security event 4688 and Sysmon event 1, with the parent process name, the command line, and network connections from the WMI provider host. Rich artefacts also exist inside WMI itself: permanent event subscriptions and consumer classes can run code on a trigger, and they persist in the repository without a file on disk, so the repository, its subscriptions, and their creation times should be baselined.

beginner.definition: Windows Management Instrumentation is a built-in Windows tool for asking the system questions and telling it to do things. Administrators use it to gather details or run jobs on many computers. Attackers use the same tool to run their own commands, sometimes on another machine.
beginner.whyItMatters: It is a normal part of Windows, so its use does not look wrong by itself. It can start programs without opening a visible command window for the user. It also works remotely, so one stolen account may be enough to reach other computers. Because it is so common in everyday administration, the warning signs are easy to miss.
howItWorks: A request is sent to the WMI service, either on the local machine or across the network.
Remote requests travel over management transports such as DCOM or WinRM on their usual ports.
The service performs the requested query or calls a method that starts a program.
The new program often appears as a child of the WMI provider host, not of a user shell.
Attackers also create permanent event subscriptions, which run code when a chosen event occurs.
Those subscriptions live inside the WMI repository rather than as a file, which hides them well.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital ward with one intercom system for the whole building. Staff use it all day to call for supplies and check on rooms. If an outsider learns the intercom code, they can order a door to be unlocked from outside the ward. The ward hears a normal announcement, because the intercom itself is genuine equipment.
takeaways: WMI runs commands through a trusted Windows service, so legitimate use and abuse look similar.
Check the parent process of new programs, since WMI-started code often has an unusual parent.
Baseline permanent WMI event subscriptions, because they survive reboots without a file on disk.

objectives: Explain what WMI is and why it can execute code both locally and remotely.
Describe the process and network artefacts created when WMI starts a program.
Identify the telemetry sources, including process creation records, that reveal WMI abuse.
Explain what a permanent WMI event subscription is and why it is a durable persistence method.
Distinguish routine administrative WMI activity from behaviour that warrants investigation.
